value_domain: Australian currency amount, dollars and cents
value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 601909, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—PBS benefit amount, total Australian currency N[NNNNN].NN' (Department of Health)
variable_description: The Commonwealth's share of what this supply cost, in dollars and cents. METeOR defines it as "the total amount of the Commonwealth government contribution towards the cost of prescription medicinal products supplied via the PBS, expressed in Australian dollars", and adds that it "equates to the total price of the prescribed medicinal product less the amount of the patient contribution". Read it against PTNT_CNTRBTN_AMT on the same row: the two add to the dispensed price, and the split between them moves with the patient's entitlement and Safety Net position rather than with the medicine. It is a payment for one supply event, so a row where RGLTN24_IND is set carries the benefit for the original script and all its repeats at once.
value_definition: Australian currency to two decimal places, in METeOR's format N[NNNNN].NN with a maximum of eight characters and cents written as .00 where there are none. The figure is the residual after the patient's contribution is taken off the dispensed price, which itself bundles the ex-manufacturer price, the wholesale mark-up and the dispensing and administration fees set in the Schedule of Pharmaceutical Benefits.
limitation: It is not the price of the medicine and not the pharmacy's revenue, so an item dispensed below the general co-payment shows 0.00 even though the medicine changed hands. It also cannot carry a continuous spend series across the whole 2006 to 2025 span: PBS collected only prescriptions that drew a subsidy until April 2012, so the zero-benefit rows that appear from then on are a change in what was collected, not a fall in average subsidy.
rationale: METeOR publishes this exact field. The PBS state/territory data extract specification (METeOR 602524) records 'Variable name = BNFT_AMT' against data element 601909, so the definition, the currency domain and the two-decimal rule apply to the column as PLIDA carries it.
evidence_quote: For a given Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription, the total amount of the Commonwealth government contribution towards the cost of prescription medicinal products supplied via the PBS, expressed in Australian dollars.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's two words 'Benefit amount' as its description, a value domain of 'Monetary amount in whole dollars (inferred)' that was wrong about the cents, and the generic sentence 'The domain is inferred from the variable name' as its definition, with a limitation that only repeated the inference warning.

value_domain: Australian currency amount, dollars and cents
value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Closing the Gap (CTG) PBS Co-payment Program' factsheet on the PBS website
variable_description: The cost of the co-payment reduction that a Closing the Gap registration attracted on this supply, in dollars and cents. Under the program a registered First Nations patient who would normally pay the full general co-payment pays the concessional rate instead, and one who would normally pay the concessional rate pays nothing, and this column holds the value of that reduction rather than the ordinary PBS subsidy, which sits in BNFT_AMT. It should be non-zero only where CTG_CD on the same row records a registration, so the two together identify supplies made under the program and what they cost the Commonwealth.
value_definition: Australian currency to two decimal places, on the same scale as the other PBS amount fields on the row. The size of a non-zero value tracks the gap between the general and the concessional co-payment, both of which are published in the Schedule of Pharmaceutical Benefits and can change on 1 January; the schedule gave $25.00 and $7.70 as at 1 July 2026.
limitation: It does not measure what the patient saved, because a concession card holder registered for the program already faced only the concessional rate and their saving is that smaller figure. It also does not identify First Nations patients: registration turns on a prescriber's judgement about chronic disease and adherence, so many First Nations patients are not registered and carry nothing here, and the column cannot stand in for an Indigenous status indicator.
rationale: METeOR publishes the Closing the Gap eligibility indicator (603679) but no data element for the benefit amount, so the field's mechanism rather than its representation is what can be sourced. The department's factsheet sets out exactly which co-payment reduction the program delivers, which is what a benefit amount on a CTG row pays for, and the currency convention is the one METeOR fixes for the neighbouring PBS amount fields.
evidence_quote: eligible First Nations people who are registered on the CTG PBS Co-payment Register and who would normally pay: the full general PBS co-payment amount, pay the concessional rate when obtaining their PBS medicines from an CTG PBS Co-payment Program approved supplier
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's phrase 'Closing the gap benefit amount' as its description and said only that the domain was inferred from the variable name, so nothing on the page explained what Closing the Gap was or why a second benefit column existed.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 602774, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—record extract date, DDMMYYYY' (Department of Health)
variable_description: The day Services Australia cut the claim file this row came out of, which is a fact about the data rather than about the patient. METeOR defines it as "the date for which the Department of Human Services (DHS) creates the file of Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) claim details for provision to the Department of Health", and notes that it "reflects a cut-off date for data records that are to be extracted from a computer system, e.g. all records processed or finalised on or before a particular date". Because PLIDA holds PBS as one table per month, this column is what put a row in its file. Use SPPLY_DT for when the medicine changed hands and PRSCRB_DT for when the script was written.
value_definition: A date, published by METeOR in DDMMYYYY form with a maximum of eight characters. Values bunch on the extract cut-off days rather than spreading through the month, because a single date covers every record in a file.
limitation: The distance between this date and the supply date is a claiming and processing lag, and METeOR warns that the lag varies from prescription to prescription, so it carries no clinical meaning. A row's presence in the table named for a month is therefore not evidence that the medicine was supplied in that month, and counting rows by this date will push late claims into the wrong period.
rationale: METeOR publishes this exact field and the PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = EXTRCT_DT' against data element 602774, so the definition and the lag warning are the custodian's own words about this column.
evidence_quote: The date for which the Department of Human Services (DHS) creates the file of Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) claim details for provision to the Department of Health, expressed as DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Date of processing' and nothing more, and its limitation described the ddmmmYY output format instead of naming the confusion between a processing date and a date of care.

value_domain: count of packs or units of use
value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 601876, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—quantity of PBS item supplied, total number N[NNN]' (Department of Health)
variable_description: How much of the item the pharmacist handed over on this supply, counted in packs or in units of use. METeOR defines the field as "the total amount of the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) item dispensed by a pharmacist, expressed either as a number of packs or units of use", and the adjustment in the name is the rule that follows it: "Where supply of the original prescription and any repeat(s) is made at the one time, pursuant to Regulation 24 of the National Health (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Regulations 1960 (Cwth), the value reported must be the total quantity supplied." A row with RGLTN24_IND set to Y therefore carries the combined quantity for the original and every repeat. What one unit means is set by the item, so ITM_CD has to be read alongside it.
value_definition: A non-negative whole number in METeOR's format N[NNN], four characters at most, with 9999 reserved for not stated or inadequately described. Whether the count is packs or units follows the item: an unbreakable pack is one pack, a breakable pack is counted in the units taken from it, and a cream or a liquid is counted in tubes or bottles rather than by volume.
limitation: It is not a dose, a volume or a days-of-supply figure, so a value of 1 can be a single tube of ointment or a pack of 30 tablets, and two rows with the same quantity can differ many-fold in the amount of drug supplied. Converting it to defined daily doses needs the pack size and strength from the Schedule of Pharmaceutical Benefits, which this table does not carry.
rationale: The PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = PBS_RGLTN24_ADJST_QTY' against METeOR data element 601876, which is the only published source that both defines the quantity and states the Regulation 24 adjustment the variable name refers to.
evidence_quote: Where supply of the original prescription and any repeat(s) is made at the one time, pursuant to Regulation 24 of the National Health (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Regulations 1960 (Cwth), the value reported must be the total quantity supplied.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's 'Quantity supplied' and a generic count limitation about the trailing token naming the unit, which is exactly wrong here: the unit is set by the item, and the RGLTN24 token in the name is about bundling, not about units.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data set specification 602524, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) state/territory data extract 2013-14' (Department of Health), DSS specific notes on the pharmacy location and remoteness items
variable_description: The postal area of the approved pharmacy that dispensed this supply and claimed for it. The PBS specification says of the matching pharmacy items that "In the context of PBS data, this data element describes the location (physical address) of the dispensing pharmacy", and that the pharmacy's published remoteness category "is based on the postcode of the pharmacy at which the prescription was dispensed", which is the postcode held here. Read against PTNT_PSTCD it shows whether a person filled the script near home, and against PRSCRBR_MJR_PSTCD whether they filled it near the prescriber. PHRMCY_ID_SCRAM says which pharmacy; this column says where it is.
value_definition: A four-digit Australian postcode. METeOR's general Australian postcode domain (data element 611398) takes its values from the Postcode datafile and reserves 0097, 0098 and 0099 for not applicable, unknown and not stated, though the PBS specification does not say which of those the extract uses.
limitation: A postcode is a postal delivery area, so it does not nest inside the ABS statistical areas and any conversion to SA2 or to remoteness runs through a correspondence that carries error. The value also belongs to the claiming approved supplier, which for a hospital pharmacy or a mail-order dispensary can sit a long way from where the patient collected the medicine, so the distance between this postcode and the patient's is a weak proxy for how far anyone travelled.
rationale: The PBS data set specification carries the department's own notes on what the pharmacy location items mean in PBS data and states that the pharmacy remoteness classification is derived from the dispensing pharmacy's postcode, which fixes what this column holds and whose address it is.
evidence_quote: In the context of PBS data, this data element describes the geographic remoteness of the dispensing pharmacy, and is based on the postcode of the pharmacy at which the prescription was dispensed.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Pharmacy postcode' twice over and gave a generic postcode limitation about four digits from 0800 to 7999, which describes the format rather than the confusion between a supplier's location and a patient's.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 602772, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—date of prescribing, DDMMYYYY' (Department of Health)
variable_description: The day the prescriber signed the script that this supply was made against. METeOR defines it as "the date on which the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescriber signs the prescription, expressed as DDMMYYYY", and notes it is "Not required for continued dispensing". Subtracting it from SPPLY_DT gives the delay between a medicine being written and being collected, which is the main use of the column. On a repeat supply the date still belongs to the original script, so one prescribing date recurs across all the rows that share a prescription.
value_definition: A date, published by METeOR in DDMMYYYY form with a maximum of eight characters. It falls on or before the supply date, and can fall well before it where a patient collected a repeat months later.
limitation: It is not the date of a consultation and is not evidence the patient saw the prescriber that day, since PBS holds no consultation record and a script can be written without a face-to-face visit; MBS is where an attendance would appear. Because METeOR exempts continued dispensing supplies from reporting it, a missing value can mark a pharmacist supply made without a prescription rather than a data fault.
rationale: METeOR publishes this exact concept for PBS and the PBS state/territory data extract specification implements it as the prescribing date on the same record as the supply date, so the definition and the continued-dispensing exemption apply to this column.
evidence_quote: The date on which the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescriber signs the prescription, expressed as DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Date of prescribing' and gave a limitation about the ddmmmYY output form, which told a reader nothing about how the date relates to the supply date or why it can be missing.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data set specification 602524, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) state/territory data extract 2013-14' (Department of Health), DSS specific notes on the prescriber location and remoteness items
variable_description: Where the prescriber did most of their Medicare work, not where this prescription was written. The PBS specification is explicit that the prescriber's location "is based on the postcode of the location at which the prescriber performed the majority of Medicare services for the most recent relevant quarter", which is what the MJR token in the name records. It is therefore a property of the doctor over a quarter rather than of the prescribing event on the row. PRSCRBR_ID_SCRAM says which prescriber wrote the script, and PRSCRBR_TYP_CD and MJR_SPCLTY_GRP_CD say what kind of practitioner they are.
value_definition: A four-digit Australian postcode from the same domain as the patient and pharmacy postcodes on the row, with values drawn from the Postcode datafile behind METeOR data element 611398.
limitation: It cannot place a prescription geographically. A specialist who consults one day a week in a regional town but bills most of their services in a capital city carries the capital's postcode on every script they write, so counts of prescribing by area understate practice in small centres. The quarterly basis also means the value can shift between one patient's rows without the prescriber having moved.
rationale: The PBS data set specification states the derivation rule for the prescriber location items in PBS data, which is the only published account of what the majority qualifier in this variable name means and the reason the postcode is not the prescribing site.
evidence_quote: In the context of PBS data, this data element describes the location (physical address) of the prescriber, and is based on the postcode of the location at which the prescriber performed the majority of Medicare services for the most recent relevant quarter.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Prescriber postcode', which is actively misleading: it invites a reader to treat the value as the place the script was written, and nothing on the page explained the MJR token or the quarterly majority-of-services rule behind it.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 605072, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—number of authorised medication supplies, total number N[N]' (Department of Health)
variable_description: How many separate supplies this one prescription authorised, which is 1 on almost every row. METeOR defines it as "the total number of times that the prescribed medicinal product is supplied to the patient or PBS consumer", and sets the rule that a repeat prescription takes "a value of 1 for those prescriptions where Regulation 24 applicable indicator has a negative response, or a value equivalent to 1 plus the number of repeats specified by the prescriber" where that indicator is positive. It rises above 1 only on the Regulation 24 rows, where the original and all its repeats went out together. Counting rows counts supply events; summing this column counts the supplies bundled inside them.
value_definition: A whole number in METeOR's format N[N], two characters at most, with 99 reserved for not stated or inadequately described. Ordinary rows carry 1, and a Regulation 24 row carries 1 plus the repeats the prescriber allowed, so a script with five repeats supplied at once carries 6.
limitation: It is not a count of prescriptions written and not a count of packs, so summing it over a patient's year gives supply occasions rather than scripts or medicines held. It also says nothing about whether the medicine was taken, and on a Regulation 24 row a whole course is dated to one day, which will distort any adherence measure built from the spacing of supplies.
rationale: The PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = PRSCRPTN_CNT' against METeOR data element 605072, whose guide for use gives the exact rule tying the value to the Regulation 24 indicator that sits on the same row.
evidence_quote: For a given Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription, the total number of times that the prescribed medicinal product is supplied to the patient or PBS consumer.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's 'Number of authorised medication supplies' and gave a generic count limitation claiming the trailing token names the unit counted, which left a reader free to read the column as a count of prescriptions.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data set specification 602524, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) state/territory data extract 2013-14' (Department of Health), DSS specific note on the patient date of birth item
variable_description: The calendar month of the patient's birth, held without a day so no row can be dated to a birthday. The PBS specification says the underlying field is the patient's date of birth and that "'Patient date of birth' is extracted from the Medicare record of the patient, as reported to the Department of Human Services (DHS)", which PLIDA splits into this column and PTNT_BRTH_YR. Taken with the year it fixes age at supply to within a month, which is what age-group analyses of dispensing rest on. It describes the person the medicine was supplied to, not the prescriber and not whoever paid.
value_definition: A month number from 1 to 12, carrying the month component of METeOR's date of birth element (287007), whose full domain is DDMMYYYY. The day component is not supplied in this asset.
limitation: On its own it gives no age, cannot order two people's births inside a month, and cannot be joined to a full date of birth held in another dataset. It also inherits whatever the Medicare enrolment holds, so a birth date estimated at enrolment leaves a month that is administrative rather than real, and there is no accuracy flag on the row to show which values those are.
rationale: The PBS data set specification names the source of the patient's birth date and its custodian, which is what determines the quality of the month PLIDA derives from it; METeOR's element 287007 fixes the underlying DDMMYYYY representation that this column is a component of.
evidence_quote: 'Patient date of birth' is extracted from the Medicare record of the patient, as reported to the Department of Human Services (DHS).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Month of birth' and its limitation only warned that the domain was inferred and that the field holds a month component, which repeated the value definition instead of naming what a month without a day cannot do.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data set specification 602524, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) state/territory data extract 2013-14' (Department of Health), DSS specific note on the patient date of birth item
variable_description: The calendar year of the patient's birth, the coarser half of the birth date PLIDA keeps for PBS. The PBS specification says of the underlying field that it "can be used to identify individual patients and may, in some use cases, need to be suppressed or perturbed", which is why only a year and a month survive here, and that it "is extracted from the Medicare record of the patient, as reported to the Department of Human Services (DHS)". Subtracting it from the year of SPPLY_DT gives age at supply to within a year, and PTNT_BRTH_MTH tightens that to a month. It is the patient's year of birth, not the year they came onto Medicare.
value_definition: A four-digit calendar year, the year component of METeOR's DDMMYYYY date of birth element (287007). Values run from the birth year of the oldest enrolled Medicare patient up to the year of the extract.
limitation: It cannot settle whether a patient had passed an age threshold on the day of supply, which matters for concession rules and for paediatric dosing, because the day of birth is gone. A year here also cannot be assumed to agree with the year of birth in Census, birth or death records: each comes from a separate enrolment or form, and the spine links people rather than reconciling the dates they reported.
rationale: The PBS data set specification identifies the Medicare record as the source of the patient's date of birth and flags it as an identifying item, which explains both where the year comes from and why PLIDA supplies only a year and a month.
evidence_quote: This data element can be used to identify individual patients and may, in some use cases, need to be suppressed or perturbed.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Year of birth' and its limitation restated that the field holds a year component, so the page never said where the birth date came from or what a missing day rules out.

value_domain: Australian currency amount, dollars and cents
value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 603362, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—PBS patient contribution, total Australian currency N[NNNNN].NN' (Department of Health)
variable_description: What the patient paid the pharmacy for this supply, on the PBS's narrow definition of a co-payment. METeOR defines it as "the total amount paid by the patient or PBS consumer to the approved pharmacy for a prescription, exclusive of any special patient contributions, e.g. brand price premiums or therapeutic group premiums", and adds that the amount "also excludes any optional fees imposed at the discretion of the pharmacy and payable by the patient". The value moves with the patient's entitlement rather than with the medicine, so it is set by PTNT_CTGRY_DRVD_CD and by whether the Safety Net threshold had been reached that calendar year. With BNFT_AMT it splits the dispensed price between the patient and the Commonwealth.
value_definition: Australian currency to two decimal places, in METeOR's format N[NNNNN].NN. The value tracks the co-payment published in the Schedule of Pharmaceutical Benefits, which METeOR says is adjusted each 1 January in line with the CPI, although statute has since frozen the concessional rate at $7.70 for 2025 to 2029: METeOR gives $36.90 for a general patient and $6.00 for a concessional patient in 2014, and the schedule's fee table gave $25.00 and $7.70 as at 1 July 2026.
limitation: It is not the money that left the patient's pocket. Brand price premiums, therapeutic group premiums and any discretionary pharmacy fee are excluded by definition, so a patient who chose a premium brand paid more than this column shows. It is also not a basis for a consistent affordability series over the whole 2006 to 2025 span, because supplies priced below the general co-payment were not collected at all until April 2012.
rationale: The PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = PTNT_CNTRBTN_AMT' against METeOR data element 603362, whose definition states precisely which charges the amount includes and excludes and whose guide for use gives the entitlement and Safety Net rules that move it.
evidence_quote: This amount also excludes any optional fees imposed at the discretion of the pharmacy and payable by the patient, e.g. fees associated with the maintenance of Safety Net records on behalf of the patient by the pharmacy.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Patient contribution amount', declared whole dollars when the field carries cents, and gave a generic limitation about losses and offsets being negative, which does not apply and hid the real trap that premiums are excluded.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data set specification 602524, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) state/territory data extract 2013-14' (Department of Health), DSS specific note on the patient state item
variable_description: The postal area of the patient's home as Medicare last recorded it, which is not necessarily where they lived when the medicine was supplied. The PBS specification says the derived patient state "is derived from 'Patient postcode', i.e. it is derived from the Medicare record of the patient and is based on the most recent patient address reported to the Department of Human Services (DHS)", and this column is that postcode. It is the geography every patient-side analysis of PBS rests on, including the remoteness categories the department publishes. Set against PHRMCY_PSTCD it shows whether the script was filled near home.
value_definition: A four-digit Australian postcode. METeOR's general Australian postcode domain (data element 611398) sources values from the Postcode datafile and reserves 0097, 0098 and 0099 for not applicable, unknown and not stated.
limitation: Medicare holds one current address rather than an address history, so an old value can be stamped on a recent supply and a move stays invisible until the person tells Services Australia. The postcode also belongs to an enrolment rather than to a residence: a child on a parent's record carries the parent's postcode, and someone living away for study or care may carry a family address. For an actual residential history the address episodes in Core Locations, keyed by ARID, are the source.
rationale: The PBS data set specification states that the patient geography items are derived from the patient postcode held on the Medicare record and describes it as the most recent address reported to the custodian, which fixes both what the column holds and why it can be stale.
evidence_quote: This data item is referred to within the PBS system as 'Patient state', and is derived from 'Patient postcode', i.e. it is derived from the Medicare record of the patient and is based on the most recent patient address reported to the Department of Human Services (DHS).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Patient postcode' twice and warned only that the domain was inferred and ran from 0800 to 7999, so nothing on the page said the address came from the Medicare enrolment or that it need not be current at the time of supply.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 602450, 'Person—sex, code A' (Department of Health), with the PBS specific note recorded against it
variable_description: The patient's sex as the Medicare entitlement record held it at the moment the claim was archived. METeOR's PBS note is explicit that "this data item is defined as being 'the gender of the consumer as held in the entitlement tables at the time the PBS claim was archived'", and warns that "gender is a social/cultural concept rather than a biological (anatomical or chromosomal) concept, although for most people the two concepts are the same". It belongs to the patient the medicine was supplied to, not to the prescriber or the cardholder. With PTNT_BRTH_YR it gives the two demographic splits available on a PBS row without leaving the table.
value_definition: A one-character alphabetic code from METeOR's Sex code A domain, covering male, female, and intersex or indeterminate, with separate supplementary codes for not stated or inadequately described and for unknown, and a blank also read as unknown.
limitation: It is a point-in-time administrative value, so a person whose Medicare record changed will carry different codes on rows before and after the change and a person-level mode will quietly erase that. It is also not comparable with the sex and gender items in Census, surveys or birth records, which are self-reported against different questions, so a disagreement between PBS and Census is not by itself evidence of a bad link.
rationale: METeOR carries both the value domain for the code and the department's own PBS specific note stating what the item means in PBS data and where it is drawn from, and the PBS state/territory data extract specification implements it as the patient sex item on the prescription record.
evidence_quote: In the context of PBS data, this data item is defined as being 'the gender of the consumer as held in the entitlement tables at the time the PBS claim was archived'.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Patient sex' with a domain of 'Sex (inferred)' and a limitation that only repeated the inference warning, so the page never said the value is an entitlement-table attribute captured at claim archive.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 601746, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—Regulation 24 applicable indicator, yes/no code A' (Department of Health)
variable_description: Whether the pharmacist was allowed to hand over the original script and all its repeats at once. METeOR defines it as "an indicator of whether supply of the original Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) item and all repeats is made at the one time", under a regulation that "allows a pharmacist to supply an original prescription medication and all of its repeats at the one time", and restricts such prescriptions to medical practitioners, midwives and nurse practitioners. Where it is positive, PRSCRPTN_CNT and PBS_RGLTN24_ADJST_QTY on the same row cover the whole bundle instead of a single supply, so this is the switch that decides how those two columns should be read.
value_definition: A one-character code with only two permissible values, one for yes and one for no, and no supplementary values published. A positive value means the prescription allowed concurrent supply of the original and every repeat; a negative one means the prescriber did not specify that.
limitation: A positive value does not mean the patient consumed the medicine over the following months, only that the pharmacy released it in one go, so treating the supply date as the start of a single short course will misdate months of treatment. It is also a poor marker of remoteness or chronic illness: those are eligibility conditions the prescriber attests to rather than facts recorded on the row, and optometrist and dental prescriptions are outside the provision altogether.
rationale: The PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = RGLTN24_IND' against METeOR data element 601746, which publishes the definition, the two-value domain and the eligibility conditions behind a positive response.
evidence_quote: An indicator of whether supply of the original Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) item and all repeats is made at the one time, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Regulation 24 applicable indicator' without saying what Regulation 24 is, and its limitation, that the field records whether a condition holds rather than its value, applied to any indicator and told a reader nothing about this one.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 602767, 'Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) prescription—date of supply, DDMMYYYY' (Department of Health)
variable_description: The day the patient took delivery of the medicine from the pharmacy, and the date a medicine-use history should be built on. METeOR defines it as "the date on which the prescribed medicinal product is supplied by a pharmacist to the patient or PBS consumer", and explains that it "essentially equates to the date of purchase", usually but not always the same as the dispensing date printed on the label. Prefer it to PRSCRB_DT, which belongs to the script, and to EXTRCT_DT, which belongs to the claim file. Each row is one supply, so a patient's repeats appear as separate rows with separate supply dates unless Regulation 24 applied and they all went out together.
value_definition: A date, published by METeOR in DDMMYYYY form with a maximum of eight characters. It falls on or after the prescribing date and on or before the extract date of the file the row sits in.
limitation: It marks the transfer of a medicine, not the start or the continuation of treatment, so it cannot show whether or when the patient took anything and a gap between supplies is only a proxy for stopping. METeOR also notes that supply and dispensing can fall on different days where a patient does not collect immediately, so the date will not always match a pharmacy's own dispensing record.
rationale: METeOR publishes this exact concept for PBS, the PBS state/territory data extract specification implements it on the prescription record, and its guide for use gives the distinction between supply, purchase and dispensing that governs how the column should be used.
evidence_quote: The date on which the prescribed medicinal product is supplied by a pharmacist to the patient or PBS consumer, expressed as DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Date of supply' and gave a limitation about the ddmmmYY output form, so the page never distinguished this date from the prescribing date or the extract date, which is the whole reason PBS carries three of them.

value_source: AIHW METeOR data element 604005, 'Prescription—repeat prescription indicator, code X' (Department of Health)
variable_description: Whether this row is the first supply against a prescription or a later one. METeOR defines the element as "an indicator of whether a prescription is a repeat prescription or an original prescription, as represented by a code", and puts the initial supply of a script that allows repeats on the original side, not the repeat side. It is what lets a patient's rows be grouped into prescriptions instead of counted as separate treatment decisions. PRVS_SPPLY_NMBR says how many supplies came earlier in this one and RPT_ORDR_NMBR how many the prescriber authorised.
value_definition: A one-character code with two published meanings: a blank marks an original prescription, including the first supply of one that allows repeats, and a single letter marks a repeat supply. The blank is a meaningful value in METeOR's domain rather than a missing one.
limitation: It does not say how far through a prescription a supply sits, so a run of repeat rows cannot be ordered without the previous-supply number, and it cannot be used to count prescriptions where Regulation 24 applied, because the original and all its repeats arrive as a single row marked as an original. A blank also does not mean the medicine was new to the patient, only that a new script had started.
rationale: The PBS state/territory data extract specification records 'Variable name = SRT_RPT_IND' against METeOR data element 604005, whose guide for use states which supply counts as original and which as repeat, and that is the fact the column turns on.
evidence_quote: This code is used where the prescription is either for the one-off supply of a medicinal product, i.e. a single bottle, packet, dose etc. of the prescribed item, or for the initial supply of a medicinal product for a prescription that allows for repeat supplies.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Repeat prescription indicator' and gave the generic indicator limitation about recording whether a condition holds, which missed both the blank-as-original convention and the way Regulation 24 rows break a naive count of repeats.

variable_description: The patient the medicine was supplied to, as the key that carries them across the whole asset. Every PBS row belongs to one person, and this is what lets a dispensing history be assembled from the monthly tables and then joined to that person's MBS services, Centrelink payments, tax records and Census responses. ABS calls the Person Linkage Spine "central to our data linking methods" and builds it from the combined population of the Medicare Consumer Directory, DOMINO Centrelink Administrative Data and Personal Income Tax records, so PBS is linked to the Spine once rather than to each dataset in turn. In this package the values are synthetic: they are consistent across tables but stand for nobody.
value_definition: An opaque identifier with no internal structure, one value per person, stable across the monthly PBS tables and across every other dataset linked through the Spine. There is no finite list to publish: the domain is as large as the Spine population, which ABS says aims to cover everyone resident in Australia at any point in the reference period, currently January 2006 to June 2025.
limitation: It identifies a person, not a prescription, a household or a Medicare card, so rows sharing a value are one patient's supplies rather than a family's, and a script filled for a child sits under the child. The bigger trap is absence: no rows in a month is not evidence that no medicine was taken, because private prescriptions, over-the-counter purchases and medicines given to public hospital inpatients never enter PBS, and a PBS record that failed to link to the Spine cannot be reached through this key at all.
rationale: The PLIDA data item list gives the field as the synthetic person identifier on every PBS table, and ABS publishes what the Spine is, which datasets it is built from, what period it covers and why datasets are linked to it once, which is what determines how this key behaves and where it can and cannot reach.
evidence_quote: The Spine aims to cover all people who were resident in Australia at any point during a given reference period. The current Spine covers January 2006 to June 2025.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's 'Synthetic MADIP Person ID' as its description and called the domain an inferred opaque identifier, with a limitation that only said there was no finite value list, so the page said nothing about the Spine, about what the key joins to, or about the coverage gaps that make an empty history misleading.
